Lessons.Title: Sums and Products of Rational and Irrational Numbers
ExplanationParagraphs: Learning goal: reason precisely about which sums and products involving rational and irrational numbers are necessarily irrational and which can become rational, identifying key exceptions. Original independent Edulytiks adaptation of Illustrative Mathematics Algebra 1 First Edition Unit 7 Lesson 21 teacher https://im.kendallhunt.com/HS/teachers/1/7/21/preparation.html and student https://im.kendallhunt.com/HS/students/1/7/21/index.html (CC BY 4.0). The source emphasizes logical arguments, not categorical guesses from limited examples.

Examples: 3+√2 is irrational because if it were rational, subtracting rational3 would make √2 rational, a contradiction. The product 3√2 is irrational because if it were rational, division by nonzero rational3 would make √2 rational. However 0·√2=0 is rational; the nonzero qualifier matters for products.

Two irrational values can have rational sum or product: √2+(−√2)=0 and √2·√2=2. They can also have irrational results, for example √2+√3 is irrational; for the latter a proof requires more than asserting both parts are irrational. A simpler clearly justified example √2+√2=2√2 is irrational. Similarly √2·√3=√6 irrational because6 is not a square.

Student task: categorize statements as always/sometimes/never true, supply either proof or counterexample, highlight the zero exception and critique statements such as 'irrational times rational is always irrational'. Teacher-scored rubric0–2 for exact examples, correct counterexamples, coherent proofs and careful quantifiers.

KeyConcepts.Title: Rational plus irrational
KeyConcepts.Definition: Adding a rational to irrational remains irrational.
KeyConcepts.Rule: If sum were rational, subtract rational term to contradict.

KeyConcepts.Title: Nonzero rational product
KeyConcepts.Definition: Multiplying irrational by nonzero rational remains irrational.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Divide by nonzero rational to prove.

KeyConcepts.Title: Two irrationals
KeyConcepts.Definition: Sum or product of two irrationals can be rational OR irrational.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Claiming irrational×rational is always irrational without exception
Inferring types of all irrational pairs from one example
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Other pairs can cancel or produce squares.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Claiming a proof from decimal approximations

SummaryPoints: Nonzero rational times irrational is irrational; zero is exception.
Two irrational operands can sum or multiply to rational numbers.
Teacher evaluates proofs, counterexamples and quantifiers.
